mcqs.question: Why does starting a Docker container typically take milliseconds while booting a VM takes tens of seconds?
options: A container is a regular process on the host's existing running kernel; a VM boots an entirely separate kernel and OS from scratch
Docker containers use a specially compiled, faster kernel that VMs don't have access to
Docker containers skip filesystem initialization entirely
VMs are always configured with more virtual CPUs, which slows down their boot sequence
mcqs.explanation: The speed difference comes from there being no second kernel to boot for a container — it's a normal process on the already-running host kernel, while a VM has to boot a full guest kernel and OS. There's no special faster kernel, filesystem setup for containers isn't skipped (image layers are still mounted), and CPU count isn't the driver of boot time.

mcqs.question: Two containers on the same host both bind to port 80 inside their own containers without conflict. Which namespace makes this possible?
options: The network namespace, since each container gets its own independent network stack including its own port space
The UTS namespace, since it isolates hostnames
The mount namespace, since it isolates filesystem paths
The user namespace, since it isolates UID mappings
mcqs.explanation: Each network namespace has its own independent set of interfaces, routing table, and port bindings, so port 80 in one namespace has no relationship to port 80 in another. Mount isolates filesystem view, UTS isolates hostname, and user isolates UID mapping — none of them govern port binding.

mcqs.question: If a container has full namespace isolation but no cgroup limits applied, what can still go wrong?
options: Nothing — namespace isolation alone is sufficient to prevent any cross-container impact
The container's filesystem would automatically become read-only
The container would be unable to start any processes at all
The container could still consume unbounded CPU or memory, starving other containers on the same host despite being isolated in view
mcqs.explanation: Namespaces isolate what a process can see, not how much of the shared hardware it can consume — without cgroup limits, a runaway process can still starve every other container for CPU or memory even though it can't see them. Namespace isolation doesn't prevent process startup and has no effect on filesystem writability.

mcqs.question: A container hits its cgroup CPU limit versus hitting its cgroup memory limit. What's the difference in what happens?
options: Hitting the CPU limit throttles the process (it keeps running, slower); hitting the memory limit typically triggers the OOM killer, which kills a process outright
Both cause the container to simply run slower, with no risk of termination
Both cause the container to be killed immediately
CPU limits are advisory and never actually enforced by the kernel
mcqs.explanation: CPU and memory limits behave very differently in practice: CPU throttling degrades performance without killing anything, while exceeding a memory ceiling normally results in the OOM killer terminating a process in the cgroup. CPU limits are enforced, not advisory, and it's specifically memory limits (not CPU) that risk an outright kill.

mcqs.question: Why can the same read-only container image safely back many running containers at once without them corrupting each other's filesystem state?
options: Docker copies the entire image for each container before it starts
The image layers are automatically locked so only one container can run from them at a time
Containers sharing an image are not allowed to write to the filesystem at all
Each container writes only to its own thin, per-instance writable layer on top of the shared read-only image layers, via copy-on-write
mcqs.explanation: overlayfs gives each container its own writable layer where modified files are copied-on-write, leaving the shared read-only image layers untouched — so many containers can run from one image simultaneously without interfering. Docker doesn't fully copy the image per container, containers can write (just not to the shared layers directly), and there's no such single-runner lock.

mcqs.question: For a genuinely untrusted, multi-tenant-hostile workload, why might a plain container be an insufficient isolation boundary compared to a VM?
options: Containers cannot be given CPU or memory limits at all
VMs don't require a kernel at all, avoiding the vulnerability class entirely
Containers are always slower than VMs, making them impractical regardless of security

All containers on a host share one kernel, so a kernel vulnerability can potentially let an attacker escape the container's namespace/cgroup restrictions entirely; a VM adds a hardware-enforced hypervisor boundary
mcqs.explanation: The shared-kernel model is the actual gap: a kernel exploit threatens every container on the host at once, while a VM's isolation rests on a separate guest kernel plus hardware-enforced hypervisor boundaries. Containers can absolutely have resource limits, containers are typically faster (not slower) than VMs, and VMs still run a real kernel — just an isolated one.

mcqs.question: A team wants to run untrusted, third-party user-submitted code with strong isolation while keeping container-like startup speed. Which approach best fits?
options: A plain Docker container with default settings, since namespaces are sufficient isolation for any workload
A traditional full VM per submission, accepting the multi-second boot cost
Running the code directly on the host with no isolation, relying on code review alone
A sandboxed runtime like gVisor or a lightweight-VM-backed runtime like Kata Containers, purpose-built to add a stronger boundary while keeping container-like speed
mcqs.explanation: gVisor and Kata exist precisely to close this gap — adding a stronger isolation boundary than a plain container's shared kernel while avoiding a full VM's boot-time cost. A default container isn't strong enough for genuinely hostile code, a full VM sacrifices the speed requirement, and running unsandboxed on the host offers no isolation at all.

mcqs.question: Why does Docker drop most Linux capabilities by default, even for a container process running as root inside the container?
options: Because 'root inside a container' would otherwise carry nearly the same broad privilege as root on the host, since it's the same kernel underneath
Because capabilities are deprecated and no longer function on modern kernels
Because dropping capabilities is required for cgroups to function correctly
Because capabilities only apply to non-root users, so root is unaffected either way
mcqs.explanation: Without dropping capabilities, a container's root user would retain most of the same broad kernel-level privileges as host root, since namespaces alone don't strip that away — dropping capabilities is what meaningfully reduces what container root can actually do. Capabilities are a live, functioning kernel feature, unrelated to cgroups' operation, and they apply to root just as much as to any other UID.
